newsitem.title: UK: Researchers rush to defence of pets.
newsitem.headline: Researchers rush to defence of pets.

text.p: Three teams of researchers rushed to the defence of pets on Friday, saying reports that they can spread illnesses such as food poisoning and lung cancer has been exaggerated.
Their reports contradicted earlier studies that indicated pet birds were linked to higher rates of lung cancer in their owners and a report that cats could spread salmonella.

Christopher Low and colleagues at the Scottish Agricultural College's veterinary services centre said they had decided to check out an August letter to the Lancet medical journal warning that cats could carry salmonella, which can cause severe food poisoning.
"Between 1991 and 1995 (our) laboratories throughout Scotland tested 1,185 feline rectal and faecal specimens, 21 of which yielded salmonella species," they wrote in the British Medical Journal.
They said this represented only one to two percent of cats. -- and sick cats who were taken to vets at that.
"We suggest that the risks of pet ownership should be kept in perspective, and that due recognition should be given to the beneficial role that pets have in society," they wrote.
Two studies in the British Medical Journal defended birds against accusations that pet birds are linked with lung cancer.
Swedish researchers from Gothenburg University studied lung cancer patients in three hospitals and concluded there was no link between the disease and keeping pet birds.
Their findings were also echoed by Saint Louis University researchers who studied all newly diagnosed cancer cases in the midwestern state of Missouri.
Their conclusion was the same: "The keeping of pet birds carries no excess risk for the development of lung cancer."
